basic.situation: A partner asks you to find which regulations apply to a client's new food delivery business. What do you do?

options.text: Search online for articles on food delivery rules and summarise what they say.
Search the statutes and regulations by topic, note the sections that apply, and check gaps with the partner.
Wait for the partner to send the regulations they want you to read first.
Search the statute database by keyword and send the partner every section you find.

advanced.situation: A client's case turns on two appeal decisions that point in opposite directions. What do you do?

options.text: Ask a senior lawyer which decision to follow.
Pick the more recent decision and build the argument on it.
Compare both decisions' facts and reasoning, then argue why ours matches the stronger one.
Search for a few more cases until one clearly settles it.

basic.situation: Your senior lawyer has a court hearing tomorrow and asks you to help prepare. What do you do?

options.text: Print the documents your senior names and bring them to court.
Put the bundle in order and flag any missing exhibits for your senior to chase.
Ask your senior what preparing for a hearing involves before you start.
Put the bundle in order, check every exhibit is there, and list questions for your senior.

advanced.situation: The other side offers a settlement an hour before a hearing, well below what your client wants. What do you do?

options.text: Weigh the offer against the likely ruling, advise the client, and counter with a figure you can justify.
Ask a senior partner to take over the negotiation before the hearing.
Advise the client on the risks and ask the other side for more time to consider.
Pass the offer to the client and let them decide whether to accept it.

basic.situation: You sit in on a client interview to record the facts of a workplace accident. What do you do?

options.text: Note the main events in order and check the spelling of names at the end.
Note dates, names and events in the client's words, and mark points the lawyer should follow up.
Write a short summary of the meeting from memory afterwards.
Listen closely and leave the note-taking to the lawyer leading the interview.

advanced.situation: A property dispute depends on who owned a plot of land in 1985, and the land office file is incomplete. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the land office to search again and wait for their reply.
Tell the client the records are incomplete and ask what they remember.
Plan a search across old title deeds, court records and gazettes, and assign who checks each source.
Search the old title deeds and court records yourself until you find the owner.

basic.situation: A client needs a simple one-year lease for a shop lot. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the senior to draft it while you watch how it is done.
Find a free lease online and send it to the senior to adapt.
Draft from the firm's lease template, fill in the client's terms, and send it for senior review.
Copy a lease from a past file, change the names and dates, and send it for review.

advanced.situation: Junior lawyers keep drafting share sale agreements with different warranty clauses. What do you do?

options.text: Write a standard warranty clause and add it to the firm's template.
Fix the clauses yourself whenever an agreement reaches you for review.
Agree a standard clause with the corporate partners and walk the juniors through when to change it.
Ask a corporate partner to remind the juniors to be more consistent.

basic.situation: A legal assistant asks you how to file a new case in the firm's records system. What do you do?

options.text: Show them the filing steps you use, then check their first entry with them.
File the case yourself so it is done correctly this time.
Show them the filing steps you use and let them try on their own.
Send them to the office manager, who looks after the records system.

advanced.situation: Your team keeps missing court filing deadlines because each lawyer tracks dates their own way. What do you do?

options.text: Raise the problem with the managing partner and wait for a decision.
Set up one shared deadline calendar and ask every lawyer to use it.
Remind the team by email before each important deadline.
Set up one shared deadline calendar, assign who checks it each week, and review misses monthly.

basic.situation: A client asks whether they must give a month's notice to leave their rented flat. What do you do?

options.text: Tell them a month's notice is usual and that they should check their agreement.
Tell them what their tenancy agreement says and ask a lawyer to confirm the law.
Tell the client a lawyer will call them back with an answer.
Check their tenancy agreement and the law, then explain their notice duty with a lawyer confirming.

advanced.situation: A large retailer asks whether a vague new data rule makes them liable for a supplier's data leak. What do you do?

options.text: Read the rule and its guidance, then advise on the reading you find most likely.
Refer them to a data protection specialist outside the firm.
Read the rule against its purpose and guidance, set out the likely readings, and advise on the safer course.
Tell them the rule is unclear and that they should wait for the regulator to clarify it.
